boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Halle entry (engagement, 17 October 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Bernadotte's 1st corps against Duke Eugen of Württemberg's Prussian reserve corps, from the French approach over the Saale bridges to the pursuit beyond Landsberg and the regiment Treskow's fight on the left bank. The Duke's retreat to Magdeburg and the detachments at Merseburg and Leipzig are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 14,500 infantry and 1,500 cavalry, 16,000 men, under Marshal Bernadotte, and side B (Prussians) 18 battalions and 20 squadrons, 11,500 infantry, 2,200 cavalry and 62 guns, 13,700 men, under General of Cavalry Duke E. of Württemberg. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner also gives about 16,000 for side A, but very nearly 11,000 for side B in action, with 2,791 of the reserve corps's infantry absent (claim hoepfner-strength); those two figures sum to 13,791 (our arithmetic), close to Bodart's 13,700, but no source read says that Bodart's figure counts the absent infantry. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 17/10. engagement at Halle (4.)'; 'victory of the French (14,500 inf., 1,500 cav. = 16,000 men) under Marshal Bernadotte over the Prussians (18 bns., 20 sqns. = 11,500 inf., 2,200 cav., 62 guns = 13,700 men) under Gen. of Cav. Duke E. of Württemberg'.

claims.value: Höpfner: in the camp at the time stood 2 grenadier and 9 musketeer battalions, 5 squadrons of dragoons, 8 squadrons of hussars, two 12-pounder batteries and half a horse battery; at the first firing the 2 companies of Knorr arrived from Leipzig, and towards noon the dragoon regiment Heyking and the 12-pounder battery Hart. With these troops and the garrison of the bridges very nearly 11,000 men went into action against about 16,000 men of the two divisions Düpont and Drouet and Marshal Bernadotte's cavalry, as 2791 men of the reserve corps's infantry were absent. The regiment Treskow, which had continued its march on Halle, sighted several columns that officers sent out reported to be enemies: it was the column of General Drouet.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page image of p. 50; it gives both sides in one sentence and does not itemise its 16,000. The print names the divisions Düpont and Drouet, while the French documents have Dupont's and Rivaud's divisions in the attack on the town and the heights and Drouet's against the column on the left bank (claim foucart-side-a); the claim keeps Höpfner's wording. Höpfner does not itemise the 2791 absent, so whether the Duke's own dispositions caused the shortfall is not established and the phase is left unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'in the camp there stood at this time — after the battalion of Jung-Larisch had returned from Leipzig at 1 o'clock in the night — still 2 grenadier and 9 musketeer battalions, 5 squadrons of dragoons, 8 squadrons of hussars, which last had left their quarters at the first cannon shot, two 12-pounder batteries and half a horse battery'; 'at the time of the first firing the 2 companies of Knorr also arrived from Leipzig, and towards noon the dragoon regiment Heyking and the 12-pounder battery Hart'; 'with these troops and the garrison of the bridges very nearly 11,000 men went into action against about 16,000 men of the two divisions Düpont and Drouet and the cavalry of Marshal Bernadotte, as 2791 men of infantry of the reserve corps were absent'; 'the regiment Treskow, which had received news of the army's defeat already at Aschersleben but had nevertheless continued its march on Halle' (OCR); 'now several columns were seen turning towards the heath. Officers sent out reported that they were enemies. It was the column of General Drouet' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B, side A's figures: Bernadotte wrote to the Emperor that his corps had set out to march on Halle and attack Duke Eugène of Württemberg, who he had just learned had arrived there 2 days before with nearly 25,000 fresh troops, the reserve of the Prussian army; that the first bridge was defended by several battalions and 4 guns; and that once master of the town he had the enemy's position, defended by 20,000 men, attacked. The corps journal, in Foucart's footnote, judged the enemy forming for battle on the heights behind the town to be 20,000 to 25,000 strong. Dupont wrote that the bridge was defended by 2,000 men and several guns; that the heights above the town were suddenly seen covered with troops, judged to be the army of the Prince of Württemberg; that this Prince had held the position for 2 days with a corps of about 30,000 men; and that the enemy, re-formed half a league from the town, was no doubt not a little astonished to see how inferior in numbers was the corps that had beaten it.
claims.rationale: Side A's reports of 18 October and the corps journal in Foucart's footnote, read from the page images except Dupont's line on the enemy re-forming (OCR); interested estimates of the enemy, not reconciled with each other, all well above Höpfner's 11,000 and Bodart's 13,700 (claims hoepfner-strength, bodart-strength). English renderings (ours): Bernadotte, 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Emperor'; 'Halle, 18 October 1806'; 'the 1st corps of the Grande Armée left yesterday at 2 o'clock in the night to march on Halle'; 'and attack Duke Eugène of Württemberg, who I had just learned had arrived there 2 days before with nearly 25,000 men of fresh troops, forming the reserve of the Prussian army'; 'General Dupont received the order to carry the town: the 32nd and a battalion of the 9th light, seconded by 3 pieces of light artillery, would make the attack on the first bridge, defended by several battalions and 4 guns'; 'once master of the town, I sent the 96th to support the 9th and 32nd, who in debouching could not have stood up to the enemy, and I had his position, defended by 20,000 men, attacked'; the journal, 'General Maison followed him to reconnoitre the enemy, who was making dispositions to defend the front of the town and the bridges, while at the same time he formed for battle on the heights that dominate it behind'; 'he was judged to be 20,000 to 25,000 men strong. (Journal of the 1st corps.)'; Dupont, 'General Dupont to Marshal Bernadotte'; 'Halle, 18 October 1806'; 'new forces were at once gathered there, so that this bridge was defended by 2,000 men and several guns'; 'at the same time the heights that dominate the town of Halle on the right bank of the Saale were suddenly seen covered with troops, and it was judged that it was the army under the orders of the Prince of Württemberg'; 'indeed this Prince had held this important position for 2 days with a corps of about 30,000 men'; 'the enemy for his part re-formed before us half a league from' (OCR); 'the town, and he was no doubt not a little astonished to see how inferior to him in number was the corps by which he had been beaten'.

claims.value: Side A in its own reports: Bernadotte had with him only 12 guns and 12 caissons for his whole corps, the rest having stayed behind at the defile of Dornburg. His order gave the attack on the first bridge to the 32e and a battalion of the 9e léger, seconded by 3 pieces of light artillery; once master of the town he sent the 96e to support the 9e and 32e, and immediately afterwards passed the 2e and 4e hussars and all Rivaud's division but a reserve battalion; the 2 divisions and the 2 hussar regiments moved on the enemy. When a column showed itself on his rear on the left bank of the Saale, Drouet's division, already recalled, arrived faster than expected, and Bernadotte ordered Drouet to have the column attacked by the 27e léger and the 95e; he had also brought up the 94e to support the great attack. Höpfner has Bernadotte order Düpont to attack with the 4 battalions of the 9th light and 32nd line regiments and keep the 2 battalions of the 96th and the hussars in reserve at Passendorf. Dupont wrote that his guns were few.
claims.rationale: Units from Bernadotte's and Dupont's letters and Höpfner, read from the page images; no source read gives a headcount for side A other than Höpfner's and Bodart's 16,000 (claims hoepfner-strength, bodart-strength). English renderings (ours): Bernadotte, 'it is well to observe to Your Majesty that I had with me only 12 guns and 12 caissons for my whole army corps, the rest having stayed behind at the defile of Dornburg'; as in claim foucart-side-b for the first attack and the 96th; 'immediately afterwards I passed the 2nd and 4th hussars and the whole division Rivaud, except for one reserve battalion'; 'the 2 divisions and the 2 hussar regiments moved on the enemy'; as in claim side-a-information for the column on the left bank; 'I had already recalled the division Drouet; this general, at the sound of the guns, had so pressed his march that he arrived much faster than could have been expected'; 'I ordered him to have the column that had appeared on our left and behind our line attacked by the 27th light and the 95th'; 'I had brought up the 94th to support the great attack'; Höpfner, 'but now Marshal Bernadotte ordered General Düpont to undertake the attack with the 4 battalions of the 9th light and the 32nd line regiments, and to leave the 2 battalions of the 96th line regiment and the hussars at Passendorf in reserve'; Dupont, 'while the enemy played his artillery on us, to which we could reply only weakly, given the small number of our guns'.

claims.value: Höpfner: Bernadotte, arrived with his corps at Querfurt, was informed there that the Duke's reserve corps lay at Halle and directed his march there to attack and beat it. Bernadotte wrote that he left Drouet's division at Unter-Teutschenthal to watch a column said to be coming from Eisleben; having reached the heights of Passendorf and seen the enemy holding the town, he judged it the moment to attack and that the town had to be taken before the Eisleben column could join the main body and before another small corps from Merseburg could join it; Dupont was ordered to carry the town, and Bernadotte gave the order not to fire but to close with the bayonet; once master of the town he sent in the 96e and had the position attacked, then passed the hussars and Rivaud's division; he had recalled Drouet, and ordered him to have the column behind his line attacked. A paragraph that Foucart prints after the journal extract in his footnote, with no attribution of its own, says Bernadotte began the attack only when Rivaud's division was debouching.
claims.rationale: The decisions as Bernadotte reported them, read from the page images, with Höpfner's account and the paragraph in Foucart's footnote from the OCR. On the page image that paragraph stands apart after the journal extract's closing attribution and carries none of its own, so it is not given as the journal's. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'Marshal Bernadotte, who had arrived on the ... in and near Querfurt with his corps in order to advance in a straight line from Weimar to Magdeburg, was informed there that the reserve corps of Duke Eugen of Württemberg was camped at Halle' (OCR); 'thought it entirely in keeping with this general order if he directed his march on Halle in order to attack and beat the Prussian corps' (as in claim side-a-objectives, OCR); Bernadotte, 'I judged it necessary to leave the division of General Drouet at Unter-Teutschenthal, pushing its cavalry regiment to Wansleben, to observe the column that was said to be coming from Eisleben to Halle'; as in claim side-a-information for the heights of Passendorf; 'I judged that it was the moment to attack and that it was absolutely necessary to seize the town before the column of Eisleben could rejoin the main corps, and also before another small corps coming from Merseburg could have made its junction'; 'I gave the order not to fire and to close with the enemy with the bayonet'; as in claims foucart-side-b and foucart-side-a for the first attack, the 96th, the hussars and Rivaud's division, Drouet's recall and the attack on the column; Foucart's footnote, 'the head of the column of the division Rivaud was beginning to appear. (Journal of the ... corps.) Marshal Bernadotte had the attack begun only at the moment when the division Rivaud was debouching and was thus within reach of supporting the division Dupont' (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart places Halle in the Prussian province of Saxony on the Saale, 32 km north-west of Leipzig. Foucart's footnote to Bernadotte's letter, attributed at its close to the corps journal: the town lies on the slope of the right bank, its wall and 4 gates dominated on that side by the crest of the hill no more than 150 toises away; several arms of the river and marshes separate it from the left bank, crossed by a dyke a quarter league long, flanked by groves and islets; on that side the town is closed by two old enclosures, each with a covered bridge before it. Bernadotte wrote that to cross all these obstacles one had to file along a dyke exposed to all the enemy's fire. Höpfner: the high bridge, the foremost walled Saale bridge, could not be defended by artillery from behind because of its high arched build, so Major Crety, arriving there, crossed it and set up his guns beyond on the dyke; the French, continually reinforced, soon pressed out at all the gates, through the gardens and over the loam walls of the suburbs. Dupont wrote that the Prince of Württemberg had batteries set up facing the gates the French had to pass, with numerous battalions adding their fire, that the ground favoured them, and that the ground the French held was commanded by the heights touching the town, which were crowned with troops.

claims.value: Höpfner: Bernadotte, arrived with his corps at Querfurt, was informed there that the Duke's reserve corps lay at Halle. Bernadotte wrote that he had just learned that the Duke had arrived at Halle 2 days before with nearly 25,000 fresh troops, that his light troops reported an enemy corps retiring on Halle by the Eisleben road, and that on reaching the heights of Passendorf he saw the enemy holding Halle in strength with a bridgehead and his whole corps crowning the heights beyond. The corps journal, in Foucart's footnote, has General Maison reconnoitre the enemy as he prepared to defend the front of the town and the bridges and formed for battle on the heights behind it; Dupont's advance guard reconnoitred the town and found the bridge held. While the fighting went on beyond Halle, a column showed itself on Bernadotte's rear on the left bank of the Saale, and a small corps, no doubt from Merseburg, sought to trouble his right flank.

claims.value: Höpfner: the King's order reached the Duke on his journey to Halle; on the onward journey he heard the cannonades of Jena and Auerstedt and concluded, from the King's letter and the fire receding, that the enemy's turning movement had been beaten off; half a day then passed without his receiving news of the previous day's battles, and the reports that came in contradicted each other; then came a report of Davout at Naumburg and Weißenfels, and a wounded officer of the regiment Renouard told him of the main army's defeat. He was also informed of the beaten army's retreat by the Halberstadt chamber, and in Höpfner's view sufficiently informed of the army's state by General Tschammer. When the attack came, a hussar officer back from patrol had reported only an hour before that nothing of the enemy had been seen near Merseburg and Lauchstädt; the dragoons' outpost was attacked so unexpectedly that the regiment was rather surprised, and the Duke took the attack for a reconnaissance.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, all from the OCR; the strength given for Davout in the report is not restated. English renderings (ours): 'Duke Eugen went in person on the ... to Halle. On the journey the royal order of the ... reached him' (OCR); 'on the further journey the Duke heard clearly the cannonades at Jena and Auerstedt, and concluded, in connection with the King's letter, as the fire receded, that the intended turning movement of the enemy had been beaten back' (OCR); 'half the ... passed without the Duke having received news of the battles of the previous day, and the news that came in contradicted each other' (OCR); 'the report came in that Marshal Davout stood with ... men in Naumburg and Weißenfels' (OCR); 'at the same time a wounded officer of the regiment Renouard arrived in Halle, who told the Duke of the defeat of the main army, the wounding of the Duke of Brunswick, his journey back etc.' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the Halberstadt chamber (OCR); 'the said order of the King however no longer made any sense, since the Duke had been sufficiently enlightened by General Tschammer about the state of the army' (OCR); 'since only an hour before a hussar officer returning from patrol had made the report that nothing of the enemy had been seen in the area of Merseburg and Lauchstädt' (OCR); 'the outpost of the regiment Herzberg dragoons had in fact been attacked so unexpectedly and thrown back on the regiment's quarters that the regiment was rather surprised' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the reconnaissance (OCR).

In his judgment the purpose of holding the crossing at Merseburg was lost once the army was beaten, and the Duke should have hurried to reach the middle Elbe at Wittenberg before the enemy. claims.value: Side B held a walled town: Bernadotte saw the enemy holding Halle in strength with a bridgehead, and reported that three bridges, two great defiles and two gates were carried; Foucart's footnote, attributed at its close to the corps journal, describes the town's wall and 4 gates and, towards the Saale, two old enclosures each with a covered bridge before it. Höpfner has the fusilier battalions returning from Merseburg stay in alarm houses in the suburbs and occupy the gates. The journal has the French in turn barricade themselves at the gates, still too weak to sally out and attack the enemy's position behind the town, until the moment to debouch; an enemy column that had pushed back the French troops defending the Ulrich gate was met in a square of the town and thrown back. Dupont writes that the Prince of Württemberg had batteries set up facing the gates the French had to pass, and that the French opened exits to the right and left of the gates. Höpfner: here too the Prussians resisted stoutly and threw the French back several times, and the French pressed from behind over the garden walls into Lange's inn close by the Ober-Galgthor and fired on the Prussians from it; continually reinforced, they soon pressed out at all the gates, through the gardens and over the loam walls of the suburbs.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the town's wall, gates and bridges were permanent works held by side B at the start, so the claim is tagged inherited. A coding that counted the French defence of the captured gates would give both_fortified, with that part gained during the action; one that counted only the fight for the position on the heights beyond the town, where the passages read name no field works, would give none_named. English renderings (ours): Bernadotte, as in claim foucart-side-b for the heading, in claim side-a-information for the bridgehead and in claim posture for the bridges and gates; the journal, as in claim halle-ground for the wall, gates and enclosures and the closing attribution; Höpfner, 'those returning from Merseburg' (OCR); '[fu]silier battalions, which arrived at ... o'clock, stayed in alarm houses in the suburbs and occupied the gates' (OCR); the journal, 'our troops, still too weak to sally and attack the position of the enemy army behind the town, barricaded themselves at the gates while waiting for the moment to debouch. (Journal of the ... corps.)' (OCR); 'arriving on one of the squares of the town, this regiment found the head of an enemy column that was entering after having pushed back our troops who defended the Ulrich gate. It at once attacked this column and threw the enemy back on his position. (Journal of the ... corps.)' (OCR); Dupont, as in claim foucart-side-b for the heading; 'the Prince of Württemberg had had batteries set up facing the gates through which we had to pass' (OCR); 'we opened ourselves exits to the right and left of the gates' (OCR); Höpfner, 'here too the Prussians put up the liveliest resistance, threw the French back several times, and here too these sought to reach their aim by pressing from behind over the garden walls into Lange's inn close by the Ober-Galgthor and firing on the Prussians from there' (OCR); 'the French, now continually reinforced, soon pressed out at all the gates, through the gardens and over the loam walls of the suburbs' (OCR).

open_questions: Deferred: the Duke of Württemberg's own report, whose loss figure Höpfner cites; Rivaud's and Drouet's reports (Dupont leaves Rivaud's division to its general's report) and the Journal du 1er corps beyond Foucart's footnotes; a French return of the losses and prisoners; Höpfner's plan of Halle and the order of battle in his footnote (pp. 44-45), whose table the OCR garbles. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the strength in the report of Davout's position (Höpfner, p. 44), the fusilier battalions back from Merseburg (p. 44), the guns with which Major Crety reached the bridge (p. 49), the regiment Treskow's companies in line (p. 57) and its dead (p. 58), the horses in General Usedom's charge (p. 54), and the dates and hours in Höpfner's and the journal's accounts.

Attribution: on Foucart's p. 100 the paragraph saying that Bernadotte began the attack only when Rivaud's division was debouching stands after the journal extract's closing attribution and has none of its own; the claims give it as Foucart's footnote, not the journal's. The description of the town in footnote 5 (pp. 99-100) is given as the journal's, since the footnote closes with that attribution.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength in action and how its loss divides between the bridge and town, the position and the regiment Treskow's column. Höpfner's 11,000 in action and Bodart's 13,700 differ by about his 2,791 absent infantry (our arithmetic), and the French estimates of 20,000 to 30,000 are far above both; a page image of Höpfner's order of battle (pp. 44-45) could give the units and their strengths.

Disputes kept as separate claims: side B's strength (very nearly 11,000 in action, Höpfner; 13,700, Bodart; nearly 25,000 and 20,000 defending the position, Bernadotte; 20,000 to 25,000, the journal; about 30,000, Dupont); the prisoners (about 5,000, Bernadotte; 4,000 to 5,000, Dupont; 4,200, Bodart; Höpfner's circa 5000 men killed, wounded, captured and missing; the Duke's total of 3000 and some hundred); the guns (at least 30, Bernadotte; about thirty, Dupont; 11 without the regimental guns, Höpfner and Bodart; 8, the Duke); side A's loss (under 800 by the French figure in Höpfner, about 800 in Bodart; 400 to 500 in Dupont's division); and the divisions Höpfner names with the cavalry (Düpont and Drouet) against the French documents' Dupont and Rivaud.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his officers, guns and flags match Höpfner's figures and his killed and wounded and French loss come close to them, by our arithmetic); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Bernadotte's and Dupont's letters of 18 October and the corps journal in his footnotes, interested accounts); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; its French loss figure is second-hand).
